addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud (requires claude.ai account access)); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	import {
2	  eligibleByCategory,
3	  REQUIRED_CATEGORIES,
4	  type CandidateItem,
5	} from "@/lib/generator/candidates";
6	import { personalBand, type Weather } from "@/lib/generator/rules";
7	import type { UiOccasion } from "@/lib/generator/types";
8	
9	/**
10	 * "A camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits" is not a query — it is a
11	 * SIMULATION. For each archetypal missing piece, add it to the real closet in
12	 * memory, re-count what becomes buildable, and report the largest increase.
13	 *
14	 * The number is produced by the same eligibility code that builds real outfits,
15	 * so it means exactly what it says rather than approximating it. No AI call.
16	 */
17	
18	/**
19	 * The archetypal pieces we know how to recommend. Deliberately small and
20	 * neutral: the claim is "this unlocks N outfits", and a wilder candidate would
21	 * inflate N while being something the user would never buy.
22	 */
23	export type GapCandidate = { label: string; category: string; colors: string[]; formality: number };
24	
25	export const GAP_CANDIDATES: GapCandidate[] = [
26	  { label: "A camel overcoat", category: "Outerwear", colors: ["camel"], formality: 4 },
27	  { label: "Grey wool trousers", category: "Bottoms", colors: ["grey"], formality: 4 },
28	  { label: "A navy knit", category: "Tops", colors: ["navy"], formality: 3 },
29	  { label: "Brown leather loafers", category: "Shoes", colors: ["brown"], formality: 4 },
30	  { label: "A white oxford shirt", category: "Tops", colors: ["white"], formality: 4 },
31	  { label: "Dark denim", category: "Bottoms", colors: ["denim"], formality: 2 },
32	  { label: "Clean white sneakers", category: "Shoes", colors: ["white"], formality: 2 },
33	];
34	
35	/**
36	 * The weather the simulation runs against: mild and dry.
37	 *
38	 * Deliberately NOT today's forecast. This screen answers "what should I buy",
39	 * and that answer must not change because it happens to be raining — a user who
40	 * checks on Tuesday and again on Thursday would be told to buy two different
41	 * things. Mild and dry also means no exclusion rule fires, so the count
42	 * measures the WARDROBE rather than the week. It is also why this screen makes
43	 * no network call of any kind.
44	 */
45	export const NEUTRAL_WEATHER: Weather = { tempC: 16, rain: false };
46	
47	/**
48	 * ⚠️ `buildCandidates` stops at `CAP = 200` (lib/generator/candidates.ts). Any
49	 * closet big enough to exceed that returns 200 both BEFORE and AFTER the
50	 * hypothetical piece, so every `unlocks` is 0 and `biggestGap` returns null —
51	 * for exactly the users who would pay for this screen.
52	 *
53	 * So do not count combos. Count the product of the eligible required slots,
54	 * which is what the cap is truncating, and is the number the claim actually
55	 * means: how many outfits become buildable.
56	 */
57	function countCombos(closet: CandidateItem[], occasions: UiOccasion[], weather: Weather): number {
58	  return occasions.reduce((total, o) => {
59	    const args = {
60	      band: personalBand(o, null),
61	      weather,
62	      // No season preference: the gap is about what the wardrobe can BUILD, and
63	      // season only ever orders and scores (see lib/generator/season.ts). A
64	      // recommendation should not change because it is currently March.
65	      season: undefined,
66	      excludeItemIds: [],
67	      maxAccessories: 0,
68	    };
69	    const by = eligibleByCategory(closet, args);
70	    const slots = REQUIRED_CATEGORIES.map((c) => (by[c] ?? []).length);
71	    // A missing required slot means zero buildable outfits, not a partial count.
72	    return total + (slots.some((n) => n === 0) ? 0 : slots.reduce((a, b) => a * b, 1));
73	  }, 0);
74	}
75	
76	/**
77	 * Which single hypothetical piece would unlock the most outfits.
78	 *
79	 * The number is produced by the SAME code that builds real outfits, so "unlocks
80	 * 14 new outfits" means exactly that — not a heuristic that resembles it.
81	 */
82	export function biggestGap(
83	  closet: CandidateItem[],
84	  occasions: UiOccasion[],
85	  weather: Weather = NEUTRAL_WEATHER,
86	): { candidate: GapCandidate; unlocks: number } | null {
87	  if (!closet.length) return null;
88	
89	  const before = countCombos(closet, occasions, weather);
90	  let best: { candidate: GapCandidate; unlocks: number } | null = null;
91	
92	  for (const c of GAP_CANDIDATES) {
93	    const hypothetical: CandidateItem = {
94	      id: "__hypothetical__",
95	      category: c.category,
96	      colors: c.colors,
97	      formality: c.formality,
98	      // Untagged on purpose: seasons, material, texture and pattern are all
99	      // "no opinion" values downstream, so the simulated piece is scored as
100	      // neutrally as possible. A hypothetical garment should not win by being
101	      // given flattering tags nobody has bought yet.
102	      seasons: [],
103	      material: null,
104	      pattern: "solid",
105	      texture: null,
106	    };
107	    const unlocks = countCombos([...closet, hypothetical], occasions, weather) - before;
108	    if (unlocks > 0 && (!best || unlocks > best.unlocks)) best = { candidate: c, unlocks };
109	  }
110	  return best;
111	}
112

1	import { formatMoney } from "@/lib/format/money";
2	import { daysBetween } from "@/lib/format/days";
3	
4	/**
5	 * The aggregates behind `/stats` (Fitcheck.dc.html:737-780).
6	 *
7	 * Pure functions over rows the caller has already fetched — no Supabase here,
8	 * so every number on that screen is testable without a database. There is no AI
9	 * call anywhere on this screen, including the gap analysis (see ./gap.ts).
10	 */
11	
12	type PricedItem = { id: string; price: number | null };
13	
14	/**
15	 * `price` is nullable and most closets are mostly null: the tagger cannot read
16	 * a price off a photograph, so it is only ever there because the user typed it.
17	 * Every total therefore has to mean "of the pieces we know about", and the
18	 * screen has to be honest that it is not the whole wardrobe.
19	 */
20	export function closetStats(
21	  items: PricedItem[],
22	  logs: { item_id: string }[],
23	): { value: string; totalWears: number; avgCostPerWear: string | null } {
24	  const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + (i.price ?? 0), 0);
25	  const totalWears = logs.length;
26	  return {
27	    value: formatMoney(total),
28	    totalWears,
29	    // Null rather than 0 or "€0.00" on either empty branch. Dividing by zero
30	    // wears prints €Infinity, and €0.00 for an unpriced closet states something
31	    // false — the UI hides the tile instead. Same stance as `itemWearStats`.
32	    avgCostPerWear: totalWears > 0 && total > 0 ? formatMoney(total / totalWears) : null,
33	  };
34	}
35	
36	/** The n most-worn item ids, highest first. Pieces with no wears are excluded. */
37	export function mostWorn(items: PricedItem[], wearsById: Record<string, number>, n: number): string[] {
38	  return items
39	    .map((i) => ({ id: i.id, wears: wearsById[i.id] ?? 0 }))
40	    .filter((i) => i.wears > 0)
41	    .sort((a, b) => b.wears - a.wears)
42	    .slice(0, n)
43	    .map((i) => i.id);
44	}
45	
46	/**
47	 * The n longest-idle pieces, with how many days it has been.
48	 *
49	 * A never-worn item is the whole point of the section, not a gap in the data —
50	 * the pieces you never reach for are exactly the ones with no wear rows. They
51	 * sort FIRST, above anything merely worn a long time ago, because "you have
52	 * never worn this" is the stronger version of the same statement.
53	 *
54	 * ⚠️ `days` is `null` for those, not `Infinity`. Infinity sorts correctly and
55	 * then reaches the screen as "∞ days ago"; null forces the UI to say "Never
56	 * worn", which is both true and the more damning line.
57	 */
58	export function gatheringDust(
59	  items: PricedItem[],
60	  lastWornById: Record<string, string>,
61	  today: string,
62	  n: number,
63	): { id: string; days: number | null }[] {
64	  return items
65	    .map((i) => {
66	      const last = lastWornById[i.id];
67	      return { id: i.id, days: last ? daysBetween(last, today) : null };
68	    })
69	    .sort((a, b) => (b.days ?? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) - (a.days ?? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY))
70	    .slice(0, n);
71	}
72

1	export type Tier = "free" | "pro";
2	
3	/** The three things that spend a model request. See docs/MONETISATION.md §2. */
4	export type GenerationKind = "drop" | "regenerate" | "styled";
5	
6	export type Entitlements = {
7	  tier: Tier;
8	  /**
9	   * Rerolls per DAY, across all occasions. null = unlimited.
10	   *
11	   * Global rather than per-occasion (user decision, 2026-08-05). Most people
12	   * care about one occasion on a given day, so a per-occasion allowance is
13	   * strictest exactly where attention goes and generous where nobody is
14	   * looking: you could be refused a second Work reroll while holding an unused
15	   * Evening one you never wanted.
16	   *
17	   * The usual objection to a global pool — that it can block an occasion you
18	   * have not opened yet — does not apply here, because a drop is free on every
19	   * tier. Tapping a new occasion is always a drop, so the pool only ever meters
20	   * rerolls.
21	   */
22	  regeneratesPerDay: number | null;
23	  /**
24	   * How many pieces a closet may hold. null = unlimited.
25	   *
26	   * Counts UNARCHIVED items only. Archiving is the user's way to make room —
27	   * there is no delete path in the product, so counting archived pieces would
28	   * strand a user at the cap with no way out. It also matches what the number
29	   * claims: an archived piece is not in your closet.
30	   *
31	   * 50 is deliberately well clear of the ~20-30 range where combo coverage
32	   * thins (PR #15 measured a 21-item closet at 21 combos in winter against 48
33	   * in summer), so the free tier never experiences a starved stylist — it
34	   * experiences a full one, with a ceiling.
35	   */
36	  closetItems: number | null;
37	  /** "Style an outfit with this" — Pro #2. */
38	  styledLooks: boolean;
39	  savedOutfits: number | null;
40	  /** The Wear Stats SCREEN. The per-item tile on item detail is free. */
41	  analytics: boolean;
42	  gapAnalysis: boolean;
43	  packingMode: boolean;
44	};
45	
46	/**
47	 * The tiers, as data. See docs/MONETISATION.md for the reasoning — in short:
48	 * meter what costs us money, sell what compounds, and never gate the daily
49	 * drop, the share card, or the closet.
50	 *
51	 * The free ceiling is four occasion drops plus three rerolls = 7 generations a
52	 * day, about $0.63/month at $0.003 each and nearer $0.20 in realistic use.
53	 * **The ceiling is the point** — a free tier needs a worst case you can
54	 * survive, and this one cannot be raised by adding clothes.
55	 */
56	export const FREE: Entitlements = {
57	  tier: "free",
58	  regeneratesPerDay: 3,
59	  closetItems: 50,
60	  styledLooks: false,
61	  savedOutfits: 10,
62	  analytics: false,
63	  gapAnalysis: false,
64	  packingMode: false,
65	};
66	
67	export const PRO: Entitlements = {
68	  tier: "pro",
69	  regeneratesPerDay: null,
70	  closetItems: null,
71	  styledLooks: true,
72	  savedOutfits: null,
73	  analytics: true,
74	  gapAnalysis: true,
75	  packingMode: true,
76	};
77	
78	// The pure functions live HERE, not in entitlements.ts, so tests can import them
79	// without dragging in `server-only` (which does not resolve under jsdom).
80	// entitlements.ts re-exports them for app code.
81	
82	/** Unknown input resolves to free: capabilities fail CLOSED. */
83	export function entitlementsFor(tier: unknown): Entitlements {
84	  return tier === "pro" ? PRO : FREE;
85	}
86	
87	export type GenerationCheck = {
88	  allowed: boolean;
89	  /** null = unlimited. Only meaningful for a metered kind. */
90	  remaining: number | null;
91	  reason?: string;
92	};
93	
94	/**
95	 * May this user spend a model request right now?
96	 *
97	 * `regeneratesUsed` is the user's total reroll count for their local today,
98	 * across every occasion.
99	 *
100	 * A drop is never metered on any tier: MONETISATION §1 and Decision 4 both say
101	 * the daily drop is the product, and rationing it is how nobody discovers the
102	 * magic. That is also what makes a global reroll pool safe — a user can always
103	 * open any occasion, so the pool can never strand them.
104	 */
105	export function checkGeneration(
106	  e: Entitlements,
107	  input: { kind: GenerationKind; regeneratesUsed: number },
108	): GenerationCheck {
109	  if (input.kind === "drop") return { allowed: true, remaining: null };
110	
111	  if (input.kind === "styled") {
112	    return e.styledLooks
113	      ? { allowed: true, remaining: null }
114	      : {
115	          allowed: false,
116	          remaining: 0,
117	          reason: "Building a look around a piece is a Pro feature.",
118	        };
119	  }
120	
121	  if (e.regeneratesPerDay == null) return { allowed: true, remaining: null };
122	  const remaining = Math.max(0, e.regeneratesPerDay - input.regeneratesUsed);
123	  return remaining > 0
124	    ? { allowed: true, remaining }
125	    : {
126	        allowed: false,
127	        remaining: 0,
128	        reason: `That's your ${e.regeneratesPerDay} rerolls for today. Pro rerolls without limit.`,
129	      };
130	}
131	
132	/**
133	 * May this user add another piece?
134	 *
135	 * `held` is the number of UNARCHIVED pieces already in the closet — archiving
136	 * is how a free user makes room, since nothing in the product deletes an item.
137	 */
138	export function checkCloset(e: Entitlements, held: number): GenerationCheck {
139	  if (e.closetItems == null) return { allowed: true, remaining: null };
140	  const remaining = Math.max(0, e.closetItems - held);
141	  return remaining > 0
142	    ? { allowed: true, remaining }
143	    : {

create table public.profiles (

  display_name    text,
  handle          text unique,
  -- style quiz (the prototype's 6 questions)

  dress_codes     text[],          -- Loungewear | Casual | Smart casual | Business | Black tie
  occasions       text[],          -- Work | Everyday | Weekend | Evening
  nogos           text[],          -- logos | skinny | bright | shorts | ripped | double_denim | graphic | square_toe
  formality_min   int default 1,   -- derived from dress_codes (for the generator's band)
  formality_max   int default 5,
  location_lat    double precision,
  location_lon    double precision,
  locale          text default 'en',
  style_dna       jsonb,
  ootd_streak     int default 0,
  onboarded_at    timestamptz,
  created_at      timestamptz default now()
);

alter table public.profiles enable row level security;

-- A user can read and update only their own profile.
-- (select auth.uid()) is the perf-optimised form; TO authenticated + ownership
-- predicate avoids the BOLA/IDOR trap; update needs both USING and WITH CHECK.
create policy "profiles_select_own"
  on public.profiles for select
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id);

create policy "profiles_update_own"
  on public.profiles for update
  to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = id)
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = id);

-- Auto-create the profile row on signup. SECURITY DEFINER so the trigger can
-- insert past RLS; schema-qualified names + empty search_path per Supabase guidance.
create function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
begin
  insert into public.profiles (id, display_name)
  values (new.id, new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'full_name');
  return new;
end;
$$;

create trigger on_auth_user_created
  after insert on auth.users
  for each row execute procedure public.handle_new_user();
